claim: DddA is a cytosine deaminase delivered via the type VI secretion system (T6SS) of Burkholderia cenocepacia.
source: Here, we examined the effects of intoxication by DddA, a cytosine deaminase delivered via the type VI secretion system (T6SS) of Burkholderia cenocepacia.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract and is supported by prior work referenced in the manuscript (Mok et al., 2020).

claim: Several bacterial species resist DddA and instead accumulate mutations.
source: Despite its killing potential, we observed that several bacterial species resist DddA and instead accumulate mutations.
evidence: This is demonstrated through bacterial competition assays and mutation frequency measurements shown in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: DddA-induced mutations can lead to the acquisition of antibiotic resistance.
source: These mutations can lead to the acquisition of antibiotic resistance, indicating that even in the absence of killing, interbacterial antagonism can have profound consequences on target populations.
evidence: This is supported by rifampicin resistance frequency data shown in Figure 4 and whole genome sequencing of resistant clones.

claim: Mutagenic activity is a common feature of deaminase superfamily toxins.
source: Investigation of additional toxins from the deaminase superfamily revealed that mutagenic activity is a common feature of these proteins, including a representative we show targets single-stranded DNA and displays a markedly divergent structure.
evidence: This is demonstrated through SNV analysis of E. coli expressing BaDTF2 and BaDTF3 toxins shown in Figure 5.

claim: DddA causes nucleoid disintegration in E. coli cells.
source: DAPI staining coupled with fluorescence microscopy revealed that the nucleoids of cells exposed to DddA rapidly disintegrate (Figure 1A and B, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is directly observed through fluorescence microscopy shown in Figure 1A and quantified in Figure 1B.

claim: DddA expression leads to genome fragmentation detectable by gel electrophoresis.
source: We further observed this phenomenon as genome fragmentation detectable by gel electrophoresis analysis of DNA extracted from cultures undergoing DddA-mediated intoxication (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is shown through agarose gel electrophoresis in Figure 1C.

claim: Uracil DNA glycosylase (Ung) initiates base excision repair by removing uracil.
source: Uracil DNA glycosylase (Ung) initiates BER by removing uracil (Yonekura et al., 2009).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from Yonekura et al., 2009.

claim: Ung inactivation leads to accumulation of uracil in DNA of DddA-intoxicated cells.
source: Employing this tool, we found that, as predicted, Ung inactivation leads to the accumulation of uracil in the DNA of DddA-intoxicated cells (Figure 1D and E, Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated through fluorescent uracil labeling shown in Figure 1D and quantified in Figure 1E.

claim: Ung inactivation alleviates nucleoid disruption and DNA fragmentation in E. coli expressing DddA.
source: Additionally, Ung inactivation alleviated both nucleoid disruption and DNA fragmentation in E. coli populations expressing DddA (Figure 1A–C).
evidence: This is shown through microscopy and gel electrophoresis data in Figure 1A-C.

claim: Deletions of genes encoding endonucleases Xth and Nfo had no impact on DddA-induced nucleoid disintegration.
source: In contrast, deletions of genes encoding the endonucleases Xth and Nfo, which operate downstream of Ung in BER by removing DNA abasic sites, had no impact on DddA-induced nucleoid disintegration.
evidence: This is demonstrated through nucleoid integrity assays shown in Figure 1A-C.

claim: E. coli wild-type and Δung are equally susceptible to DddA intoxication.
source: However, we found that E. coli wild-type and Δung were equally susceptible to intoxication (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is shown through viable cell counts in Figure 2A.

claim: DddA induction results in rapid loss of fluorescent foci formed by YPet-labeled DnaN in both wild-type and Δung E. coli strains.
source: In both wild-type and Δung E. coli strains, DddA induction resulted in the rapid loss of fluorescent foci formed by YPet-labeled DnaN, an established indicator of replication fork collapse (Aakre et al., 2013; Reyes-Lamothe et al., 2010; Figure 2B–D, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and B, Video 1 and Video 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated through time-lapse microscopy shown in Figure 2B-D and Videos 1 and 2, with citation to established methods.

claim: Genomic DNA sequencing of E. coli Δung after DddA expression revealed widespread C•G-to-T•A transitions in the preferred context for DddA (5'-TC-3').
source: However, genomic DNA sequencing at this time point revealed widespread C•G-to-T•A transitions in the preferred context for DddA (5'-TC-3'), consistent with the uracil enrichment we observed by fluorescent labeling (Figure 1D and E, and Figure 2E–G).
evidence: This is shown through SNV analysis in Figure 2E-G.

claim: E. coli does not exhibit DddA-mediated inhibition when grown in competition with B. cenocepacia.
source: Surprisingly, we found no evidence of DddA-mediated inhibition of E. coli in these experiments.
evidence: This is demonstrated through bacterial competition assays shown in Figure 3A.

claim: A B. cenocepacia strain lacking T6SS-1 activity (∆icmF) exhibits reduced competitiveness toward E. coli.
source: However, we observed that a B. cenocepacia strain lacking T6SS-1 activity (∆icmF) exhibits reduced competitiveness toward E. coli, indicating that toxin delivery can occur between these organisms.
evidence: This is shown through competition assays in Figure 3A.

claim: The effect of DddA delivery via T6SS varies among different Gram-negative organisms.
source: We found that the effect of DddA delivery via the T6SS varied; in general, enteric species and Acinetobacter baumannii (Figure 3A and B) resisted intoxication, whereas other species, including Pseudomonas aeruginosa, P. putida, and other Burkholderia species (Figure 3C and D), were highly sensitive to DddA-mediated killing.
evidence: This is demonstrated through competition assays shown in Figure 3A-D.

claim: E. coli populations subject to intoxication by T6SS-1 of wild-type B. cenocepacia for a single hour display a nearly 10-fold increase in the frequency of rifampicin-resistant cells compared to those exposed to B. cenocepacia dddAE1347A.
source: Strikingly, we found that E. coli populations subject to intoxication by T6SS-1 of wild-type B. cenocepacia for a single hour display a nearly 10-fold increase in the frequency of rifampicin-resistant (RifR) cells compared to those exposed to B. cenocepacia dddAE1347A (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is shown through mutation frequency measurements in Figure 4A.

claim: In 24 of 25 rifampicin-resistant E. coli clones from competition with B. cenocepacia, resistance was conferred by C•G-to-T•A transitions within the preferred context of DddA.
source: Sequencing of rpoB from 25 independent clones obtained from E. coli populations grown in competition with B. cenocepacia revealed that in all but one of these, rifampicin resistance was conferred by C•G-to-T•A transitions within the preferred context of DddA (Figure 4B, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is shown through rpoB sequencing data in Figure 4B and Supplementary file 1.

claim: There is significant enrichment for C•G-to-T•A transitions in the 5′-TC-3′ context in rpoB of DddA-intoxicated E. coli populations compared to spontaneous RifR mutants.
source: In contrast, a study of 152 spontaneous RifR mutants in E. coli found only 32 such mutations in rpoB (Garibyan et al., 2003), indicating significant enrichment for this sequence signature in clones deriving from DddA-intoxicated populations (Fisher's exact test, p<0.001).
evidence: This is demonstrated through statistical comparison with published data from Garibyan et al., 2003.

claim: Whole-genome sequencing of 10 RifR E. coli clones revealed 12 additional mutations outside of rpoB, all of which were C•G-to-T•A transitions in a 5′-TC-3′ context.
source: Whole-genome sequencing (WGS) of 10 RifR clones isolated from these experiments led to the identification of an additional 12 mutations outside of rpoB distributed across these strains, and all were C•G-to-T•A transitions in a 5′-TC-3′ context (Figure 4B and C, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is shown through whole genome sequencing data in Figure 4B-C and Supplementary file 1.

claim: K. pneumoniae and enterohemorrhagic E. coli (EHEC) display higher RifR frequency when in contact with B. cenocepacia containing active DddA than with B. cenocepacia bearing the dddAE1347A allele.
source: Among the resistant organisms, Klebsiella pneumoniae and enterohemorrhagic E. coli (EHEC) displayed higher RifR frequency when in contact with B. cenocepacia containing active DddA than when in contact with B. cenocepacia bearing the dddAE1347A allele (Figure 4D and E)
evidence: This is shown through mutation frequency measurements in Figure 4D and E.

claim: Within 11 K. pneumoniae isolates sequenced, 50 of 51 SNPs detected were C•G-to-T•A transitions in the 5′-TC-3′ context preferred by DddA.
source: Within the 11 K. pneumoniae isolates we sequenced, 50 of the 51 SNPs detected were C•G-to-T•A transitions, and each of these was located in the 5′-TC-3′ context preferred by DddA (Mok et al., 2020), a highly significant enrichment compared to spontaneous mutation patterns (p<0.001) (Lee et al., 2012).
evidence: This is shown through whole genome sequencing data with statistical analysis comparing to spontaneous mutation patterns from Lee et al., 2012.

claim: In EHEC isolates, 82 of 88 SNPs across seven strains corresponded to C•G-to-T•A transitions in the context preferred by DddA.
source: The EHEC isolates we sequenced shared this trend, with 82 of 88 SNPs across seven strains corresponding to C•G-to-T•A transitions in the context preferred by DddA.
evidence: This is shown through whole genome sequencing data in Figure 4H-I and Supplementary file 1.

claim: There is no indication of clustering of DddA-induced mutations across genomes of E. coli, K. pneumoniae, or EHEC.
source: We found no indication of clustering of DddA-induced mutations across genomes of E. coli, K. pneumoniae, or EHEC, suggesting that mutagenesis by the toxin occurs in a random fashion (Figure 4C,F and I).
evidence: This is shown through genome distribution plots in Figure 4C, F, and I.

claim: There is no evidence of increased mutation frequency in populations of B. cenocepacia K56-2, B. ambifaria, and P. aeruginosa that are susceptible to DddA killing.
source: We observed no evidence of increased mutation frequency in populations of the susceptible competitors B. cenocepacia K56-2, B. ambifaria, and P. aeruginosa (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C–E).
evidence: This is shown through mutation frequency measurements in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C-E.

claim: Intoxication of P. aeruginosa ∆ung by DddA yields elevated mutation frequency, resembling that of Enterobacteriaceae exposed to the toxin.
source: However, intoxication of P. aeruginosa ∆ung by DddA yielded elevated mutation frequency, resembling that of Enterobacteriaceae exposed to the toxin (Figure 4—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This is shown through mutation frequency measurements in Figure 4—figure supplement 1F.

claim: Eight deaminase superfamily subfamilies possess members associated with interbacterial toxin systems.
source: Aravind and colleagues describe 22 sequence divergent subfamilies into which enzymes belonging to the deaminase superfamily distribute (Iyer et al., 2011). Among these, eight subfamilies possess members associated with interbacterial toxin systems (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is based on bioinformatic analysis from Iyer et al., 2011 and shown in Figure 5A.

claim: P. syringae WP_011168804.1 (BaDTF2) and T. equigenitalis WP_044956253.1 (BaDTF3) exhibit toxicity when heterologously expressed in E. coli.
source: Like DddA, both exhibited toxicity when heterologously expressed in E. coli (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is shown through toxicity assays in Figure 5B.

claim: BaDTF2 and BaDTF3 representatives introduce high levels of C•G-to-T•A transitions when expressed in E. coli.
source: Remarkably, despite their sequence divergence from DddA, representatives from both BaDTF2 and BaDTF3 introduced high levels of C•G-to-T•A transitions (Figure 5C–F).
evidence: This is shown through SNV analysis in Figure 5C-F.

claim: The BaDTF2 representative preferentially targets cytosine within pyrimidine tracks (5'-YCY) but can also deaminate cytosines in all other contexts with lower efficiency.
source: The BaDTF2 representative preferentially targeted cytosine located within pyrimidine tracks (5'-YCY), but could also deaminate cytosines in all other contexts with lower efficiency (Figure 5G).
evidence: This is shown through sequence logo analysis in Figure 5G.

claim: The BaDTF3 member targets cytosine most efficiently when preceded by thymidine, and less efficiently when preceded by adenosine or cytosine; it does not act on cytosines preceded by guanosine (5'-HC).
source: In contrast, the BaDTF3 member targeted cytosine most efficiently when preceded by thymidine, and less efficiently when preceded by adenosine or cytosine; it did not act on cytosines preceded by guanosine (5'-HC) (Figure 5H).
evidence: This is shown through sequence logo analysis in Figure 5H.

claim: The BaDTF2 protein (SsdA) exhibits potent cytosine deaminating activity toward single-stranded DNA.
source: Unlike DddA, the BaDTF2 protein exhibited potent cytosine deaminating activity toward ssDNA (Figure 5I).
evidence: This is shown through in vitro deamination assays in Figure 5I.

claim: SsdA targets cytosine residues in double-stranded DNA with considerably lower efficiency than single-stranded DNA.
source: Cytosine residues in dsDNA were also targeted, but with considerably lower efficiency (Figure 5J).
evidence: This is shown through in vitro deamination assays in Figure 5J.

claim: Purified SsdAtox can target cytosine residues preceded by any of the four bases.
source: Consistent with the in vivo mutagenesis results, purified SsdAtox could target cytosine residues preceded by any of the four bases (Figure 5K).
evidence: This is shown through in vitro deamination assays in Figure 5K.

claim: SsdAtox exhibits only residual activity toward RNA targets in vitro.
source: Notably, we detected only residual activity of SsdAtox toward RNA targets in vitro, suggesting that DNA is the physiologically relevant substrate of the toxin (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is shown through poisoned primer extension assays in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: RNA-seq analysis of E. coli cells expressing SsdAtox revealed no detectable increase in the number of C•G-to-T•A transitions in cDNA sequences.
source: This is supported by RNA-seq analysis of E. coli cells expressing SddAtox, which revealed no detectable increase in the number of C•G-to-T•A transitions in cDNA sequences (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B and C).
evidence: This is shown through RNA-seq analysis in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B and C.

claim: The structure of SsdA in complex with SsdAI was determined to 3.0 Å resolution.
source: To begin to understand the basis for the distinct substrate preference exhibited by SsdA, we determined its structure in complex with its immunity determinant, SsdAI, to 3.0 Å (Figure 6A and Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is stated directly and shown in Figure 6A with crystallographic data in Supplementary file 2.

claim: The structure of SsdA exhibits the basic characteristics of deaminase enzymes, including active site histidine and cysteine residues in position to coordinate a zinc ion.
source: The structure of SsdA exhibits the basic characteristics of deaminase enzymes, including active site histidine and cysteine residues in position to coordinate a zinc ion, and the five β-strands (S1-5) and three α-helices (H1, H3, and H4) that constitute the core fold of deaminase superfamily enzymes (Figure 6B; Iyer et al., 2011).
evidence: This is shown through structural analysis in Figure 6B with reference to Iyer et al., 2011.

claim: SsdA groups with the C-terminal hairpin division of the deaminase superfamily.
source: More specifically, SsdA groups with the C-terminal hairpin division of the superfamily, and consistent with this assignment, S4 and S5 of SsdA are antiparallel.
evidence: This is based on structural analysis and comparison with deaminase superfamily classification from Iyer et al., 2011.

claim: SsdA bears little structural homology with characterized deaminases, including DddA.
source: Outside of its basic fold, SsdA bears little structural homology with characterized deaminases, including DddA (Figure 6C–E).
evidence: This is shown through structural comparison in Figure 6C-E.

claim: SsdA bears most overall structural similarity with the folate-dependent transformylase domain of PurH (DALI Z score, 7.7).
source: Indeed, SsdA bears most overall structural similarity with the folate-dependent transformylase domain of PurH (DALI; Z score, 7.7), which contains the deaminase fold despite its sequence and functional divergence from deaminase enzymes (Iyer et al., 2011; Wolan et al., 2002).
evidence: This is based on DALI structural comparison analysis with references to Iyer et al., 2011 and Wolan et al., 2002.

claim: SsdAI is an exclusively α-helical protein that shares a large (~1300 Å2) interface with SsdA.
source: SsdAI is an exclusively α-helical protein that shares a large (~1300 Å2) interface with SsdA.
evidence: This is determined from the crystal structure shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The SsdA-interacting surface of SsdAI effectively demarcates the active site of SsdA.
source: As is often observed in toxin–immunity co-crystal structures, this interface effectively demarcates the active site of SsdA (Figure 6A; Hernandez et al., 2020).
evidence: This is shown in the structure in Figure 6A with reference to general principles from Hernandez et al., 2020.

claim: SsdAI residues contact a conserved Ser-Gly-Trp (SGW) motif that resides in close proximity to the active site of SsdA and is unique to the BaDTF2 members of the DYW subgroup.
source: Interestingly, these residues contact a conserved Ser-Gly-Trp (SGW) motif that resides in close proximity to the active site of SsdA and is unique to the BaDTF2 members of the DYW subgroup.
evidence: This is shown through structural analysis in Figure 6D and F, and sequence analysis in Figure 6G.

claim: Several conserved features of DYW proteins important for mitochondrial or chloroplast gene editing in vivo are absent from BaDTF2 proteins.
source: Our search revealed several conserved features of DYW proteins previously demonstrated to be important for mitochondrial or chloroplast gene editing in vivo that are absent from the BaDTF2 proteins. These include the eponymous C-terminal DYW residues, a CxC motif believed to be important for coordinating a second Zn2+ atom, and a proline-glycine (PG) motif located within a characteristic insertion between S2 and H2 of the deaminase fold (Figure 6G; Boussardon et al., 2014; Gutmann et al., 2020; Wagoner et al., 2015).
evidence: This is shown through sequence analysis in Figure 6G with references to Boussardon et al., 2014; Gutmann et al., 2020; Wagoner et al., 2015.

claim: BaDTF2 proteins contain a conserved SGW motif within the insertion between S2 and H2 of the deaminase fold, instead of the PG motif found in DYW proteins.
source: Instead, BaDTF2 proteins contain the aforementioned SGW motif within this insertion.
evidence: This is shown through sequence analysis in Figure 6G.

claim: DddA is a double-stranded DNA-targeting cytosine deaminase.
source: We recently demonstrated that one of these proteins, a substrate of an interbacterial toxin-delivering T6SS of Burkholderia cenocepacia, acts as a double-stranded DNA-targeting cytosine deaminase (Mok et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated with reference to prior work from Mok et al., 2020.

claim: DddA's activity of targeting double-stranded DNA stands in contrast with all previously characterized DNA-targeting deaminases, which act preferentially on single-stranded substrates.
source: This unusual activity stands in contrast with all previously characterized DNA-targeting deaminases, which act preferentially on single-stranded substrates.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about previously characterized deaminases.

claim: DddA is highly toxic when expressed heterologously in E. coli.
source: We also showed that unlike the housekeeping deaminases APOBEC3G, TadA, and Cdd, this protein, which we named DddA (double-stranded DNA deaminase A), is highly toxic when expressed heterologously in Escherichia coli.
evidence: This is stated with reference to prior work from Mok et al., 2020.

claim: Cytosine deamination generates uracil, which is removed from DNA by the base excision repair (BER) pathway.
source: Cytosine deamination generates uracil, which is removed from DNA by the base excision repair (BER) pathway (Wallace, 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from Wallace, 2014.

claim: The presence of abasic sites in close proximity on opposite DNA strands can lead to double-strand DNA breaks.
source: This process generates abasic sites and previous reports indicate that the presence of these lesions in close proximity on opposite strands can lead to double-strand DNA breaks (D'souza and Harrison, 2003).
evidence: This is cited from D'souza and Harrison, 2003.

claim: Pathways for the delivery of toxins into contacting cells are widespread in bacteria.
source: Pathways for the delivery of toxins into contacting cells are widespread in bacteria. These include the type IV-VI secretion systems (T4-T6SS) in Gram-negative bacteria, the Esx secretion system of Gram-positives, and a number of specialized mechanisms that display a more limited distribution (Klein et al., 2020; García-Bayona et al., 2017; Jamet et al., 2015; Koskiniemi et al., 2013; Vassallo et al., 2017).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from multiple references.

claim: Within populations of toxin-producing strains, self-intoxication is prevented through the production of specific immunity determinants that neutralize individual toxins.
source: Within populations of toxin-producing strains, self-intoxication is prevented through the production of specific immunity determinants that neutralize individual toxins (Hernandez et al., 2020).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from Hernandez et al., 2020.

claim: In Burkholderia thailandensis, a CDI toxin causes increased expression of more than 30 genes in resistant cells, including those encoding exopolysaccharide biosynthesis proteins and a T6SS.
source: However, in Burkholderia thailandensis, it was demonstrated that a toxin delivered by the contact-dependent inhibition pathway (CDI) causes increased expression of more than 30 genes in resistant cells, including those encoding exopolysaccharide biosynthesis proteins and a T6SS (Garcia et al., 2016).
evidence: This is cited from Garcia et al., 2016.

claim: Within a population of CDI toxin-producing bacteria, some cells fail to completely neutralize incoming CDI toxins, leading to induction of the stringent response and enhanced antibiotic tolerance via growth arrest.
source: A separate study found that within a population of CDI toxin-producing bacteria, some cells fail to completely neutralize incoming CDI toxins delivered by their neighbors, leading to induction of the stringent response, and ultimately to enhanced antibiotic tolerance via growth arrest of this sub-population (Ghosh et al., 2018).
evidence: This is cited from Ghosh et al., 2018.

claim: Whether toxin delivery can impact the long-term evolutionary landscape of target cell populations has not been explored.
source: Whether toxin delivery can impact the long-term evolutionary landscape of target cell populations has not been explored.
evidence: This is stated as a gap in knowledge that the current study addresses.

claim: Proteins that catalyze the deamination of bases in nucleotides and nucleic acids are found in all domains of life and play essential roles in a range of physiological functions.
source: Proteins that catalyze the deamination of bases in nucleotides and nucleic acids are found in all domains of life and play essential roles in a range of physiological functions (Iyer et al., 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from Iyer et al., 2011.

claim: Bioinformatic analyses revealed that a large and diverse collection of predicted bacterial and archaeal deaminases exhibit hallmarks of substrates of antibacterial toxin delivery pathways.
source: Bioinformatic analyses of the origins of the deaminase fold led to the surprising finding that a large and diverse collection of predicted bacterial and archaeal deaminases exhibit hallmarks of substrates of antibacterial toxin delivery pathways, including the T6SS, the Esx secretion system, and the CDI pathway (Iyer et al., 2004; Makarova et al., 2019).
evidence: This is cited from Iyer et al., 2004 and Makarova et al., 2019.

claim: dddA is encoded in only 97 of 308 B. cenocepacia strains with publicly available genomes.
source: Given that dddA is encoded in only 97 of 308 B. cenocepacia strains with publicly available genomes and is missing from widely employed model strains of this species (J2315 and K56-2), we also evaluated whether it could mediate intoxication of a strain lacking the effector gene and its accompanying immunity determinant, dddAI.
evidence: This is based on bioinformatic analysis of publicly available genomes.

claim: B. cenocepacia K56-2 was susceptible to DddA intoxication to a level similar to other Burkholderia species tested.
source: We found that this strain, B. cenocepacia K56-2, was susceptible to intoxication to a level similar to other Burkholderia species tested (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is shown through competition assays in Figure 3D.

claim: In all sensitive bacteria tested, DddA accounted for all the inhibitory activity of the T6SS of B. cenocepacia under the conditions of the assay.
source: Notably, in all the sensitive bacteria, DddA accounted for all the inhibitory activity of the T6SS of B. cenocepacia under the conditions of our assay.
evidence: This is inferred from competition assays shown in Figure 3C-D where dddAE1347A mutant shows no inhibitory activity.

claim: The susceptibility of P. aeruginosa to DddA intoxication was not influenced by ung inactivation.
source: Interestingly, the susceptibility of P. aeruginosa to DddA intoxication was not influenced by ung inactivation (Figure 3G), consistent with our earlier conclusion that cell death mediated by the toxin occurs upstream of massive uracil accumulation and widespread chromosome fragmentation (Figure 1).
evidence: This is shown through viability assays in Figure 3G.

claim: Salmonella enterica and Acinetobacter baumannii did not exhibit increased RifR frequency when exposed to B. cenocepacia with active DddA.
source: Among the resistant organisms, Klebsiella pneumoniae and enterohemorrhagic E. coli (EHEC) displayed higher RifR frequency when in contact with B. cenocepacia containing active DddA than when in contact with B. cenocepacia bearing the dddAE1347A allele (Figure 4D and E); Salmonella enterica and Acinetobacter baumanii did not exhibit this behavior (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This is shown through mutation frequency measurements in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: The genomes of 65 RifR P. aeruginosa clones derived from interbacterial growth competition experiments revealed mutations exclusively within rpoB, with only 15% conforming to the mutagenic signature of DddA.
source: Furthermore, the genomes of 65 RifR P. aeruginosa clones derived from interbacterial growth competition experiments between P. aeruginosa and B. cenocepacia revealed mutations exclusively within rpoB, and only 15% of these mutations conformed to the mutagenic signature of DddA (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is shown through whole genome sequencing data in Supplementary file 1.

claim: Mutagenesis is likely a rare outcome of DddA-mediated intoxication in sensitive competitor species.
source: These results suggest that mutagenesis is likely a rare outcome of DddA-mediated intoxication in sensitive competitor species, but raise the possibility that it may become more frequent in strains unable to repair DddA-catalyzed lesions in DNA.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that susceptible species show little mutagenesis unless ung is deleted.

claim: Previously characterized proteins in the DYW deaminase family are found in plants and protists and participate in C to U editing of specific organellar mRNA transcripts.
source: Previously characterized proteins in the DYW deaminase family are found in plants and protists and participate in C to U editing of specific organellar mRNA transcripts (Hayes and Santibanez, 2017; Oldenkott et al., 2019; Shikanai, 1847).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from Hayes and Santibanez, 2017; Oldenkott et al., 2019; Shikanai, 1847.

claim: In DYW proteins from plants and protists, the DYW deaminase domain is generally found at the C-terminus of a larger polypeptide characterized by pentatricopeptide repeats (PPRs), which recruit the catalytic domain to target mRNAs.
source: In these organisms, the DYW deaminase domain is generally found at the C-terminus of a larger polypeptide characterized by pentatricopeptide repeats (PPRs), which recruit the catalytic domain of the protein to target mRNAs (Barkan and Small, 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from Barkan and Small, 2014.

claim: The structure of SsdA-SsdAI places the PG motif region in position to engage substrate.
source: In this regard, our structure of the SsdA–SsdAI complex likely provides some insights. For example, it places the PG motif region, which differs markedly between BaDTF2 and DYW proteins, in position to engage substrate.
evidence: This is inferred from the crystal structure shown in Figure 6.

claim: DddA displays significantly greater structural relatedness to eukaryotic deaminases targeting ssDNA (AID/APOBEC) than it does to SsdA.
source: Despite the predicted shared ancestry of DddA and SsdA, DddA displays significantly greater structural relatedness to eukaryotic deaminases targeting ssDNA (AID/APOBEC) than it does to SsdA.
evidence: This is based on structural comparison analysis.

claim: Cytosine deaminases targeting single-stranded DNA evolved at least twice from the ancestral deaminase fold.
source: Taken together, this suggests that cytosine deaminases targeting ssDNA evolved at least twice from the ancestral deaminase fold (Iyer et al., 2011).
evidence: This is inferred from structural comparisons with reference to Iyer et al., 2011.

claim: The toxicity of SsdA could result from targeting highly transcribed genes that are more likely to exist in a single-stranded state.
source: One explanation may be that because highly transcribed genes are more likely to exist in a single-stranded state, the toxicity of SsdA could result from the targeting of these specific regions.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning about the mechanism of SsdA toxicity.

claim: The lower level of dsDNA targeting by SsdA observed in vitro may represent the physiologically relevant activity of the protein during cellular intoxication.
source: Alternatively, the lower level of dsDNA targeting by SsdA that we observe in vitro may represent the physiologically relevant activity of the protein during cellular intoxication.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning about the mechanism of SsdA toxicity.

claim: Thymine starvation leads to cell death in organisms from E. coli to humans, in a process known as thymineless death (TLD).
source: While nutrient deprivation typically results in growth arrest, thymine starvation induced through genetic inactivation or chemical inhibition of thymine biosynthesis leads to cell death in organisms from E. coli to humans, in a process known as TLD (Khodursky et al., 2015; Hanawalt, 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from Khodursky et al., 2015 and Hanawalt, 2015.

claim: Both TLD and DddA intoxication involve the incorporation of uracil into DNA and produce complex phenotypes including DNA replication arrest and chromosome degradation.
source: There remains no consensus on the precise mechanism of TLD, but it is nevertheless possible to draw parallels between TLD and DddA intoxication. Both processes involve the incorporation of uracil into DNA and produce complex phenotypes including DNA replication arrest and chromosome degradation (Khodursky et al., 2015).
evidence: This is based on comparison with established knowledge about TLD from Khodursky et al., 2015.

claim: For both TLD and DddA intoxication, the removal of uracil incorporated into DNA does not rescue cells from intoxication.
source: Also, for both TLD and DddA intoxication, the removal of uracil incorporated into DNA does not rescue cells from intoxication (Sangurdekar et al., 2010).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 2A and comparison with TLD literature from Sangurdekar et al., 2010.

claim: Suppressor mutants resistant to killing by TLD appear to be difficult to obtain.
source: More generally, suppressor mutants resistant to killing by TLD appear to be difficult to obtain (Fonville et al., 2011; Guzmán and Martín, 2015).
evidence: This is cited from Fonville et al., 2011 and Guzmán and Martín, 2015.

claim: The indelible signature that deaminase toxins leave within the genomes of target cells offers a unique opportunity to study bacterial interactions in nature.
source: In this regard, the indelible signature that deaminase toxins leave within the genomes of target cells offers a unique opportunity. Future studies aimed at mining genomic and metagenomic datasets for sequence signatures indicative of deaminase toxin activity have the potential to provide heretofore unobtainable insights into the complexities of bacterial interactions in nature.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning about future research directions.

claim: Under certain circumstances hypermutator phenotypes proliferate within bacterial populations.
source: There is strong evidence that under certain circumstances hypermutator phenotypes proliferate within bacterial populations (Barrick and Lenski, 2013; Mena et al., 2008; Denamur et al., 2000).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from Barrick and Lenski, 2013; Mena et al., 2008; Denamur et al., 2000.

claim: In hypermutator cells, the fitness contribution of beneficial mutations outweighs the reduction on fitness by other, deleterious mutations.
source: In such cells, the fitness contribution of beneficial mutations outweighs the reduction on fitness by other, deleterious mutations (Denamur and Matic, 2006; Jayaraman, 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from Denamur and Matic, 2006 and Jayaraman, 2011.

claim: In spatially structured, cooperating bacterial systems, hypermutator phenotypes could be transiently achieved with the aid of neighboring cells via the delivery of a mutagenic toxin.
source: In spatially structured, cooperating bacterial systems, it is conceivable that such hypermutator phenotypes could be transiently achieved with the aid of neighboring cells via the delivery of a mutagenic toxin.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning about the ecological role of mutagenic toxins.

claim: A toxin that acts as a mutagen of a cooperating bacterium could also remain as a component of the antibacterial arsenal of the producer.
source: Additionally, our data show that the same deaminase toxin can mutagenize certain bacteria while causing death in others. Therefore, a toxin that acts as a mutagen of a cooperating bacterium could also remain as a component of the antibacterial arsenal of the producer.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that DddA has different effects on different species.

claim: DNA repair pathways may provide one source of diversity in determining cell fate following intoxication by DddA.
source: This suggests that the determinants of cell fate following intoxication by DddA frequently vary between species. DNA repair pathways may provide one relevant source of diversity.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on observed species differences.

claim: mug orthologs are present across Enterobacteriaceae but not found in most Pseudomonads.
source: Interestingly, mug orthologs are not universal among bacteria; the gene is present across Enterobacteriaceae, but it is not found in most Pseudomonads (Brunder and Karch, 2000; Silby et al., 2011).
evidence: This is cited from Brunder and Karch, 2000 and Silby et al., 2011.

claim: Recognition and turnover of DddA via cellular proteolytic machinery is one potential source of stochasticity in determining cell fate.
source: Recognition and turnover of DddA via cellular proteolytic machinery is one potential source of this stochasticity. In the majority of cells belonging to a resistant species, proteolytic machinery may fortuitously and effectively deplete DddA; however, in a small subset of these cells, this machinery might fail to act before DddA installs one or more mutations.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning about mechanisms of resistance.

claim: Killing of target cells by interbacterial antagonistic systems can rely on the delivery of exceedingly small numbers of toxin molecules – in some cases as few as one.
source: Killing of target cells by interbacterial antagonistic systems can rely on the delivery of exceedingly small numbers of toxin molecules – in some cases as few as one (Cascales et al., 2007).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from Cascales et al., 2007.

claim: C•G-to-T•A transitions are often reported as the most common mutation type observed within evolving bacterial populations.
source: Studies often report C•G-to-T•A transitions as the most common mutation type observed within evolving bacterial populations.
evidence: This is stated as general knowledge from the literature.

claim: Spontaneous cytosine deamination is implicated in the GC skew observed between leading and lagging strands on bacterial chromosomes.
source: Nevertheless, they do provide some insights into the origins of cytosine mutations in natural contexts, as they implicate spontaneous cytosine deamination in the GC skew observed between leading and lagging strands on bacterial chromosomes (Bhagwat et al., 2016).
evidence: This is cited from Bhagwat et al., 2016.

claim: DddA can install multiple mutations on a single genome during one intoxication event.
source: For instance, based on the ability of DddA to install multiple mutations on a single genome during one intoxication event, deaminase toxins may facilitate the emergence of phenotypes that are otherwise slow to evolve.
evidence: This is inferred from whole genome sequencing data showing multiple mutations per clone in Figure 4.

claim: Resistance to certain antibiotics requires a succession of mutagenic events.
source: This could be clinically relevant to the treatment of polymicrobial infections, where bacteria that possess deaminase toxins are present and the resistance to certain antibiotics requires a succession of mutagenic events (Cabot et al., 2014; van der Putten et al., 2019).
evidence: This is cited from Cabot et al., 2014 and van der Putten et al., 2019.

claim: The activity of only one DYW protein has been reconstituted in vitro.
source: Although there is substantial evidence implicating DYW proteins in RNA editing, little of this is direct and to our knowledge the activity of only one DYW protein has been reconstituted in vitro (Hayes and Santibanez, 2017).
evidence: This is stated as a gap in knowledge with reference to Hayes and Santibanez, 2017.

claim: Coordinates and structure factors for SsdA/SsdAI complex have been deposited in the Protein Data Bank (PDB) under accession code 7JTU.
source: Coordinates and structure factors for SsdA/SsdAI complex have been deposited in the Protein Data Bank (PDB) under accession code 7JTU.
evidence: This is stated directly in the Materials and methods section.

claim: Sequencing data associated with this study have been deposited at the NCBI Trace and Short-Read Archive (SRA) under BioProject accession ID PRJNA659516.
source: Sequencing data associated with this study have been deposited at the NCBI Trace and Short-Read Archive (SRA) under BioProject accession ID PRJNA659516.
evidence: This is stated directly in the Materials and methods section.
